scope_note: Research module outside the nine-document core corpus. Categories are culture- and period-specific; modern Western labels are not assumed to be exact equivalents.

records.claim: Bugis society is documented in modern ethnographic scholarship as recognizing five gender categories rather than only two.
records.qualification: The five categories are not interchangeable and should be researched individually; the numeric summary must not substitute for their distinct social and ritual meanings.

sources.author: Sharyn Graham Davies
sources.title: Challenging Gender Norms: Five Genders among Bugis in Indonesia

records.claim: Published research describes fa'afafine as a locally recognized alternative gender-role category distinct from normative man and woman categories in Samoa.
records.qualification: Individual studies use Western analytical labels such as transgender or third gender; those labels are not treated as exact translations of fa'afafine.

sources.author: Paul L. Vasey and Nancy H. Bartlett
sources.title: What can the Samoan 'Fa'afafine' teach us about the Western concept of gender identity disorder in childhood?

sources.author: Paul L. Vasey et al.
sources.title: Traits of separation anxiety in childhood: a retrospective study of Samoan men, women, and fa'afafine

records.period: modern, with deeper South Asian historical context pending
records.claim: Khawaja Sira in Pakistan are documented as a heterogeneous gender-nonconforming community, with umbrella terminology that contains important internal distinctions.
records.qualification: Legal recognition after Pakistani Supreme Court directives is a separate legal layer and does not prove a single uniform identity across all people covered by umbrella terms.

sources.author: Muhammad Azfar Nisar
sources.title: Governing Thirdness: State, Society, and Non-binary Identities

records.period: historical nation-specific traditions; modern umbrella from 1990
records.claim: Scholarship documents many nation-specific Indigenous gender and sexuality categories; Two-Spirit is a modern umbrella term adopted in 1990 rather than the historical name of every tradition.
records.qualification: Future records must identify the specific nation/community and local term. Do not collapse distinct traditions into one pan-Indigenous historical category.

sources.author: Gregory D. Smithers
sources.title: Reclaiming Two-Spirits: Sexuality, Spiritual Renewal & Sovereignty in Native America

sources.author: Sue-Ellen Jacobs, Wesley Thomas, and Sabine Lang, eds.
sources.title: Two-Spirit People: Native American Gender Identity, Sexuality, and Spirituality

records.claim: Kathryn M. Ringrose argues that Byzantine eunuchs functioned in a distinct gender configuration that cannot be reduced to a simple male/female social binary, especially in urban courtly contexts.
records.qualification: This is Ringrose's modern historical interpretation of Byzantine evidence, not a claim that Byzantines used today's gender vocabulary.

sources.author: Kathryn M. Ringrose
sources.title: The Perfect Servant: Eunuchs and the Social Construction of Gender in Byzantium

records.place: Biomedical classification; Britain case study for medical history
records.claim: Sex is a multidimensional construct involving multiple anatomical and physiological traits, which do not always align in one typical male or female pattern; twentieth-century medicine increasingly classified and surgically managed people with atypical sex characteristics.
records.qualification: Intersex is not itself a third-gender category. Gender identity and social classification must be recorded separately from variations in sex traits.

sources.author: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
sources.title: Measuring Sex, Gender Identity, and Sexual Orientation

sources.author: David Andrew Griffiths
sources.title: Diagnosing sex: Intersex surgery and 'sex change' in Britain 1930–1955

sources.author: Luke Muschialli et al.
sources.title: Perspectives on conducting 'sex-normalising' intersex surgeries conducted in infancy: A systematic review

records.period: cuneiform evidence across multiple periods; especially 2nd–1st millennia BCE
records.claim: Cuneiform evidence supports an unconventional gender performance associated with the assinnu in the cult of Ištar, including transgression of ordinary gender boundaries.
records.qualification: Svärd and Nissinen caution that evidence does not justify treating castration, same-sex sexual role, or a modern transgender identity as settled facts. Their analysis distinguishes gender performance from sexuality and from modern identity categories.

sources.author: Saana Svärd and Martti Nissinen
sources.title: (Re)constructing the Image of the Assinnu

sources.author: Ilan Peled
sources.title: Visualizing Masculinities: The Gala, Hegemony, and Mesopotamian Iconography

records.claim: Hatshepsut, a woman who ruled as pharaoh, was represented in some official sculpture in the idealized masculine form and regalia of Egyptian kingship while inscriptions retained feminine grammatical forms and her female personal name.
records.qualification: This demonstrates gendered conventions of royal office and representation, not evidence that Hatshepsut belonged to a third-gender social category or was attempting to conceal that she was a woman.

sources.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.title: Hatshepsut in a Devotional Attitude

sources.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.title: The Female Pharaoh Hatshepsut

records.claim: Deuteronomy 23:1 excludes a man with crushed or severed genitalia from the assembly of YHWH, while Isaiah 56:3–5 promises covenant-keeping eunuchs a place and enduring name in God's house.
records.qualification: This is a direct textual contrast inside the biblical corpus. It does not by itself establish a third-gender category, and historical dating or causation requires separate scholarship.

sources.author: Hebrew Bible
sources.title: Deuteronomy 23:1

sources.author: Hebrew Bible
sources.title: Isaiah 56:3–5

records.claim: Rabbinic legal texts explicitly discuss persons who cannot be classified as definitely male or female in particular legal contexts, including tumtum and androgynos.
records.qualification: Calling the rabbinic system 'six genders' is a modern shorthand that can mislead. Scholarship describes these categories as strongly body- and legal-status-based, and shows that rabbinic law often manages ambiguity relative to a structurally important male/female binary.

sources.author: Jane L. Kanarek
sources.title: Rewriting 'Arakhin: Women and Tannaitic Vows of Valuation
sources.locator: AJS Review 40.2, pp. 261–277; discussion of M. Arakhin 1:1

sources.author: Marianne Schleicher
sources.title: Constructions of Sex and Gender: Attending to Androgynes and Tumtumim Through Jewish Scriptural Use

records.claim: The galli, priests of Cybele/Magna Mater, were associated with self-castration and feminine-coded clothing and appearance, and Roman literary portrayals often treated them as violating normative masculinity.
records.qualification: Some modern scholars interpret the galli as nonbinary or outside expected gender binaries. That is a modern analytical interpretation; ancient self-identification is not recoverable, and surviving literary sources are frequently hostile.

sources.author: Chris Mowat
sources.title: Don't be a Drag, Just be a Priest: The Clothing and Identity of the Galli of Cybele in the Roman Republic and Empire

sources.author: Marika Rauhala
sources.title: Obscena Galli Praesentia: Dehumanizing Cybele's Eunuch-Priests through Disgust

records.claim: Canon 1 of the Council of Nicaea distinguished involuntary or medically necessary castration from voluntary self-castration: involuntary/medical eunuchs could remain or be admitted to clergy if otherwise worthy, while clergy who voluntarily castrated themselves were to cease ministry and such candidates were not to be promoted.
records.qualification: This is an institutional rule about castration and clerical eligibility. It should not be converted into a claim about the person's gender identity.

sources.author: First Council of Nicaea
sources.title: Canon 1

records.claim: Philo of Alexandria repeatedly uses eunuchism and castration in exegetical and philosophical discussions of male and female categories; modern scholarship treats these passages as important evidence for Philo's gender hierarchy and symbolic use of eunuchism.
records.qualification: This is evidence about Philo's exegesis and philosophical anthropology, not proof that Alexandrian Jews recognized eunuchs as a third social gender.

sources.author: Ra‘anan Abusch
sources.title: Eunuchs and Gender Transformation: Philo’s Exegesis of the Joseph Narrative

records.place: Early Christianity / Roman eastern Mediterranean literary context
records.claim: Acts 8 repeatedly identifies an Ethiopian royal official as a eunuch and depicts his baptism without narrating a change in that bodily/social designation.
records.qualification: Brittany Wilson argues that the figure is gender-, ethnicity-, and status-ambiguous in Greco-Roman context and embodies boundary crossing. That is a scholarly interpretation of the narrative, not a recovered self-identification.

sources.author: Brittany E. Wilson
sources.title: ‘Neither Male nor Female’: The Ethiopian Eunuch in Acts 8.26–40

records.claim: Matthew 19:12 distinguishes eunuchs born so, eunuchs made so by others, and those who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom; Eusebius later reports that Origen interpreted the verse literally enough to castrate himself.
records.qualification: The Matthew text is direct evidence. The historicity of Origen's self-castration is debated in modern scholarship, so the Origen episode is kept as disputed reception history rather than certain biography.

sources.author: New Testament
sources.title: Matthew 19:12

sources.author: Eusebius
sources.title: Ecclesiastical History, Book VI

sources.author: Ronald E. Heine
sources.title: Origen and his Opponents on Matthew 19:12

records.claim: Rabbinic texts classify aylonit and forms of saris through bodily signs, fertility, and legal consequences rather than treating all persons as simply typical male or typical female bodies.
records.qualification: Sarra Lev argues that the constructed bodily signs cross sex/gender markers, while also noting that rabbinic law generally does not treat the aylonit as a separate gender identity. These are legal/body classifications, not a direct equivalent of modern trans or intersex identities.

sources.author: Sarra Lev
sources.title: How the 'Aylonit Got Her Sex

records.claim: The Kāmasūtra explicitly describes persons of a 'third nature' and distinguishes two forms, including one characterized by feminine dress, speech, manner, and a specific sexual/economic role.
records.qualification: The text provides a named category outside ordinary male/female erotic roles, but the category is embedded in ancient Sanskrit sexual taxonomy and should not be mapped automatically onto modern transgender or gay identities.

sources.author: Vātsyāyana
sources.title: Kāmasūtra
sources.locator: 2.9.6–24; trans. Wendy Doniger and Sudhir Kakar, Oxford University Press, 2002

sources.author: Wendy Doniger
sources.title: The Third Nature: Gender Inversions in the Kamasutra

records.claim: Mughal khwāja sarās were enslaved, castrated court officials who could hold important positions in elite households and political space; surviving naming, dress, office, and textual evidence generally categorized them as men.
records.qualification: Emma Kalb stresses that 'eunuch' has been used too broadly in South Asian historiography. Mughal khwāja sarās should not be collapsed into the distinct hijra community or treated automatically as a third gender.

sources.author: Emma Kalb
sources.title: A eunuch at the threshold: mediating access and intimacy in the Mughal world
sources.locator: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 33.3, pp. 747–768

records.claim: Part II of the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871 created registers of persons the colonial state classified as 'eunuchs', penalized registered persons for appearing publicly in feminine dress or performing, and restricted their ability to act as guardians or adopt children.
records.qualification: The colonial statutory category 'eunuch' did not map cleanly onto Hijra identity. Jessica Hinchy's archival work shows that officials sought the gradual elimination of Hijra public visibility and social reproduction, while actual enforcement varied and Hijras resisted and evaded control.

sources.author: British Indian colonial legislature
sources.title: Criminal Tribes Act, 1871

sources.author: Jessica Hinchy
sources.title: Governing Gender and Sexuality in Colonial India: The Hijra, c.1850–1900

sources.author: Jessica Hinchy
sources.title: Obscenity, Moral Contagion and Masculinity: Hijras in Public Space in Colonial North India

records.claim: British colonial administration used the English category 'eunuch' to group distinct South Asian populations and defined the legal category in male terms, including persons 'of the male sex' judged impotent.
records.qualification: This was a colonial administrative classification, not a neutral translation of one indigenous identity. Hinchy argues that the category rendered diverse people legible to the colonial state as failed or deviant men and obscured differences among Hijras, khwāja sarās, zenanas, and others.

sources.title: Criminal Tribes Act, 1871
sources.locator: Definition and registration provisions in Part II

sources.title: Power, perversion and panic: eunuchs, colonialism and modernity in North India

sources.title: Governing Gender and Sexuality in Colonial India: The Hijra, c.1850–1900

records.claim: Spanish missionary and military sources described Indigenous people who dressed and worked in feminine-coded roles, often under the colonial label joya, and condemned these practices while expressing an expectation that missionization would eliminate them.
records.qualification: Joya was a colonial umbrella label that collapsed distinct nation-specific terms and roles. Deborah Miranda characterizes the suppression as 'gendercide'; that term is treated as her interpretation rather than the site's unqualified label for every California community.

sources.author: Deborah A. Miranda
sources.title: Extermination of the Joyas: Gendercide in Spanish California

sources.author: Diana Roselly Pérez Gerardo
sources.title: Hombres que vivían como las mujeres en la Alta California del siglo XVIII: Coyas/joyas, cuút o uluqi, ¿sodomitas, hermafroditas o amaricados?

sources.author: Mario Alberto G. Magaña Mancillas and Raúl Balbuena Bello
sources.title: Joyas o indios vestidos de mujer en la Alta California colonial: reflexiones sobre la identidad de género

records.place: United States federal Indian boarding schools
records.claim: Federal Indian boarding schools imposed sex-segregated dress, labor, domestic training, and Victorian gender norms as part of forced assimilation.
records.qualification: This was one mechanism among many in settler colonial assimilation. The effect on specific Indigenous gender systems varied by nation, school, period, family, and individual; the record also documents resistance rather than complete cultural erasure.

sources.author: K. Tsianina Lomawaima
sources.title: Domesticity in the federal Indian schools: the power of authority over mind and body

sources.author: David Wallace Adams
sources.title: Education for Extinction: American Indians and the Boarding School Experience, 1875–1928

sources.author: Teresa Evans-Campbell, Karina L. Walters, Cynthia R. Pearson, and Christopher D. Campbell
sources.title: Indian Boarding School Experience, Substance Use, and Mental Health among Urban Two-Spirit American Indian/Alaska Natives

records.claim: Protestant missionaries promoted permanent sexually exclusive heterosexual marriage and a more patriarchal domestic model in Hawai‘i, contributing to changes in gender and sexual relations during the early nineteenth century.
records.qualification: Sally Engle Merry emphasizes that this transformation was multicausal and negotiated: missionaries, Hawaiian chiefs, foreign commerce, demographic catastrophe, political change, and existing Hawaiian institutions all shaped the outcome. This record does not yet make a māhū-specific suppression claim.

sources.author: Sally Engle Merry
sources.title: Early Pacific Encounters and Masculinity: War, Sex, and Christianity in Hawai‘i

records.claim: British clinicians were performing surgical interventions on people with atypical sex characteristics before the Johns Hopkins protocols associated with John Money became internationally influential.
records.qualification: The history is not a simple before/after story. Griffiths shows that British clinicians used surgery, hormones, social sex, gonadal sex, psychology, and welfare-state ideas in changing combinations. John Money was influential but did not invent intersex surgery.

sources.author: David Andrew Griffiths
sources.title: Diagnosing sex: Intersex surgery and 'sex change' in Britain 1930–1955

records.claim: John Money, Joan G. Hampson, and John L. Hampson published formal recommendations in 1955 on sex assignment, change of sex, and psychological management for people then described as hermaphroditic.
records.qualification: Later historical scholarship describes the Hopkins approach as emphasizing early assignment, consistent gender rearing, and surgical conformity, but also shows that its genealogy was transatlantic and built on earlier clinical practices rather than arising fully formed from one researcher.

sources.author: John Money, Joan G. Hampson, and John L. Hampson
sources.title: Hermaphroditism: recommendations concerning assignment of sex, change of sex and psychologic management
sources.locator: Bulletin of the Johns Hopkins Hospital 97(4):284–300

sources.author: Sandra Eder
sources.title: Gender and Cortisone: Clinical Practice and Transatlantic Exchange in the Medical Management of Intersex in the 1950s

sources.author: David Andrew Griffiths
sources.title: Diagnosing sex: Intersex surgery and 'sex change' in Britain 1930–1955

records.claim: Intersex patient activism in the 1990s challenged secrecy, stigma, and unwanted genital surgery; the 2006 international medical consensus explicitly recognized patient-advocacy and ethical concerns and proposed 'disorders of sex development' as new clinical terminology.
records.qualification: The 2006 terminology was itself contested and did not end debate over surgery, consent, or the medicalization of intersex traits. The record tracks an institutional shift, not a completed resolution.

sources.author: Intersex Society of North America
sources.title: What's the history behind the intersex rights movement?

sources.author: Peter A. Lee et al.
sources.title: Consensus Statement on Management of Intersex Disorders

records.claim: New York City rules for changing sex designations on birth certificates changed substantially between 1965 and 2006, with administrative reasoning shifting from fraud prevention toward evidence of permanence.
records.qualification: This case demonstrates the historical construction of legal sex criteria in one jurisdiction. It should not be generalized to all U.S. states or all identity documents.

sources.author: Paisley Currah and Lisa Jean Moore
sources.title: ‘We Won't Know Who You Are’: Contesting Sex Designations in New York City Birth Certificates

records.claim: German civil-status law evolved from allowing a blank sex entry for some people, to a 2017 constitutional ruling requiring a positive option beyond male/female when sex registration is mandatory, to the 2018 'divers' entry and a 2024 self-determination law allowing changes among available gender-marker options or deletion of the marker.
records.qualification: Eligibility and legal effects changed across these reforms. The 2017 constitutional case concerned a person with atypical sex development; the 2024 Self-Determination Act established a broader identity-based procedure and should not be retroactively read into the earlier law.

sources.author: German Federal Constitutional Court
sources.title: Order of 10 October 2017, 1 BvR 2019/16

sources.author: Deutscher Bundestag
sources.title: Birth register amendment adding 'divers'

sources.author: Federal Republic of Germany
sources.title: Act on Self-Determination With Regard to Gender Markers (SBGG)

records.claim: Nepal has officially recognized a third-gender/'other' category in state documents since implementation of the 2007 Supreme Court decision, and current passport instructions provide M, F, and X options tied to the applicant's citizenship certificate.
records.qualification: The legal category 'other' and passport marker X are administrative categories, not proof that all Nepali people who use them share one identity or social role.

sources.locator: Notes official recognition since 2007 and citizenship 'other' category

records.claim: Passport sex/gender marker policy differs across states: as of 28 September 2026 the United States issues only M or F matching sex at birth and no X marker, while Australia and New Zealand continue to provide X marker options under their passport systems.
records.qualification: This is a dated policy snapshot, not a permanent rule. U.S. policy is actively shaped by executive action and litigation; Australia and New Zealand use their own definitions and eligibility procedures.

sources.title: Sex Markers in Passports

records.claim: Ifi Amadiume documents Nnobi institutions in which women could occupy socially masculine kinship and political positions described analytically as 'male daughters' and 'female husbands', showing that sex did not mechanically determine every social role.
records.qualification: Amadiume's broader thesis about precolonial African gender has been highly influential and debated. The record treats 'male daughter' and 'female husband' as kinship/status roles, not automatically as modern gender identities or evidence of one continent-wide African gender system.

sources.author: Ifi Amadiume
sources.title: Male Daughters, Female Husbands: Gender and Sex in an African Society

sources.author: Lorelle Semley
sources.title: When We Discovered Gender: A Retrospective on Ifi Amadiume’s Male Daughters, Female Husbands

records.claim: Regina Smith Oboler documents Nandi women who married wives, paid bridewealth, managed family property, and became the social/legal fathers of their wives' children in order to secure heirs.
records.qualification: The institution is primarily about kinship, inheritance, property, and fatherhood. It should not automatically be interpreted as lesbian marriage or a distinct gender identity, even though Nandi informants described the female husband as becoming socially male in important contexts.

sources.author: Regina Smith Oboler
sources.title: Is the Female Husband a Man? Woman/Woman Marriage among the Nandi of Kenya

records.period: modern ethnography with older historical roots
records.claim: Rudolf Gaudio documents 'yan daudu as a recognized category of feminine men in Hausa Muslim society with distinctive social networks, speech practices, occupations, and relationships to women's spaces and bori traditions.
records.qualification: The category intersects gender expression, sexuality, class, religion, and urban life. It should not be reduced to a simple Western category such as gay man, trans woman, or third gender.

sources.author: Rudolf Pell Gaudio
sources.title: Allah Made Us: Sexual Outlaws in an Islamic African City

records.period: late Indigenous era reconstruction through contemporary scholarship
records.claim: Douglas Oliver's reconstruction of late Indigenous Tahitian society reports institutionalized tolerance for anatomically male people who adopted female behavioral roles, identified as māhū; later scholarship distinguishes māhū from raerae and traces how these categories changed through family life, tourism, colonialism, and globalization.
records.qualification: Oliver's account is a historical reconstruction based heavily on early-contact sources, not a transparent transcript of pre-contact self-understanding. Modern māhū and raerae categories are not assumed to be unchanged survivals from the eighteenth century.

sources.author: Douglas L. Oliver
sources.title: Ancient Tahitian Society

sources.author: Niko Besnier
sources.title: Polynesian Gender Liminality Through Time and Space

sources.author: Makiko Kuwahara
sources.title: Living as and Living with Māhū and Raerae: Geopolitics, Sex, and Gender in the Society Islands

records.claim: Ethnographic scholarship documents fakaleitī as a recognized Tongan category involving feminine presentation and social roles among people assigned male.
records.qualification: Fakaleitī identities and life strategies are heterogeneous and shaped by Tongan kinship, sexuality, religion, migration, and global media. The term is not treated as a direct synonym for a Western transgender identity.

sources.author: Mary K. Good
sources.title: The Fokisi and the Fakaleitī: Provocative Performances in Tonga

sources.author: Niko Besnier
sources.title: Transgenderism, Locality, and the Miss Galaxy Beauty Pageant in Tonga

records.claim: Tom Boellstorff documents waria as a widely recognized Indonesian feminine-male/transfeminine social category embedded in Indonesian national culture.
records.qualification: Boellstorff explicitly argues that waria are better understood in their Indonesian context than simply labeled a universal 'third gender'; he describes the category as a form of male femininity and analyzes its relationship to national ideas of authenticity.

sources.author: Tom Boellstorff
sources.title: Playing Back the Nation: Waria, Indonesian Transvestites

unresolved.claim_under_test: At least one culture recognized seven or more distinct gender categories.
unresolved.publication_rule: Do not publish a numeric claim until a culture-specific, period-specific source establishes the categories and their meanings.

unresolved.claim_under_test: Historical actors used reproductive difference as an argument that social gender must be exhaustively binary.
unresolved.publication_rule: Trace the argument in named texts, laws, institutions, or thinkers; do not infer causation from the existence of binary legal categories alone.
